title: Producer Dardo's idea of a tap dancers' lineup
summary: The Curly McDimple producer, a Capezio salesman, needed a new show, and Green suggests assembling many tap dancers on stage as he had seen at the Apollo.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans

blocks.x: But so, Mr. Dardo, he says, say, you know, I got a Monday here --

It's a dark night. He said, I really would like to turn it into another show, you know, because they're trying to -- they're threatening me with some kind of lawsuit. And he said, I'm going to reverse the charges (unintelligible). "Dames at Sea," you see, because they wrote -- they write story -- they were story writers. And he and Mary were author and co-author, you see. And he needed more finan-

So he said -- he seemed to like tap dancing. He said you're a very good tap dancer, but you don't dance -- you don't tap dance like George Hillman. I said, well, no, darn, I said well I'm his teacher, you see. See. Said I used to be -- we were just room buddies, I says. And he and his brother and I were very good friends. We was on a long tour, you see, with Don Redman, you understand. The jazz giant little giant. Jazz giants.

And so, he says that he liked tap dancing. He said, 'What do you think I should do?' (unintelligible). He said, 'What kind of show would I use?' He says 'I wants to teach these people a lesson by trying to disturb deformation (unintelligible) being fraudulent, you see. In other words, they're trying to -- like "Dames at Sea" now, he had -- see, they tried to take his story idea, you know, and he wasn't having it. And his mother -- I mean she was kind of ill at the time, afflicted. But everybody -- Like I said, it was a family story. That's on and (unintelligible) off stage, you see.

And so, I said, 'Well, I know some tap dancers. We had been on a tap dance night up there at the Apollo Theater and (unintelligible) Theatre House up in Harlem down on 125 Street.' And I said 'Well now -- there was quite a number of us on the stage. We was in a lineup, you know.' I said we was, you know -- I said 'The Russians come here. And what do you call those horse riders? They comes and they -- the more
people that they'd see on stage during something of the same, you know, the more audiences enjoyed themselves." I said, "It would be good for tourists, you know.

So, he said, "Well, you know, I don't know too much about tap dancing." By the way, Mr. Dardo was in some movies, you know. And he used to work for Capezio. He was a salesman in the Capezio up here on Broadway in Fun Foreign City. Awfully nice for a person, you know. Everybody liked him, as I say.

But now, the Dixie Theater -- I mean the Dixie -- I mean there Burt Wheeler Theater, we used to be a club called the Plantation, you see. And it was -- Woolsey -- Charles Woolsey -- I mean he got to be the president of the Showmans, the theatrical organization, you know. And he made his partner a president of this theater, you know -- Burt Wheeler Theater.
